sec.title: Abstract
Abstract
sec.p: Many old American radio recordings survive today. Collectors trade the recordings as sound files. A large number of the recordings carry no date. Often the only information about a recording is the file name. File names do not last. People write the file name again at every copy. Computers cut the file name short. When a file name is hard to read, a cataloger chooses a date. So the date is lost, and many surviving dates are wrong.

The paper describes a method for finding the true date of a radio recording. The main evidence is the newspaper radio log — the daily list of radio programs printed in American newspapers. The method compares radio logs from several separate newspapers. The method also uses trade magazines, and evidence inside the recording.

The paper reports what the method produced at The Archive of American Radio. The Archive of American Radio holds 259,915 broadcast records across 6,114 programs. Twenty-eight percent of the 259,915 records still have no date.

The paper also proposes a way to mark how strong the evidence is for each date. The mark separates a date proved by several independent listings from a date a cataloger only chose, and from a date passed along by another collection and never tested.

The paper gives an example. Six independent listings move the date of a *Greatest Story Ever Told* recording by almost seven years. The day of the week cannot settle the question, because both possible dates fall on a Sunday, and *Greatest Story Ever Told* aired on Sundays.

The paper reports a limit as well. In the sample studied, the number of listings available for a broadcast rises sharply with the year across the 1930s. The measure of the rise is a correlation of 0.899 across fourteen records. Evidence is not equally thick across the whole period. Any dating system must show where evidence is thick and where evidence is thin, and must not hide the difference behind a flat claim of fact.
**Keywords:** old-time radio, discography, broadcast dating, newspaper radio logs, sound records, audio archives, metadata

A considerable body of American radio broadcasting survives as sound recordings, and the surviving material circulates among private collectors as digital audio files. A significant proportion of the surviving material carries no broadcast date, and in many instances the only documentation accompanying a recording is the file name. File names are inherently unstable: file names are rewritten at each transfer, shortened by the operating systems responsible for storage, and, where the text can no longer be read, replaced by a cataloger's estimate. The date is therefore lost, and a significant share of the surviving dates are demonstrably erroneous.

The present paper specifies a method for establishing the true broadcast date of an undated recording. The primary evidence is the newspaper radio log, the day-by-day schedule of radio programs printed in American daily newspapers, and the method derives authority from the comparison of newspaper radio logs published independently in several cities. Trade press listings and evidence internal to the recording itself supplement the newspaper radio log.

The paper reports the results obtained through the application of the method at The Archive of American Radio, a published catalog of 259,915 broadcast records distributed across 6,114 programs. Twenty-eight percent of the 259,915 broadcast records remain undated.

The paper further proposes a framework for making the strength of the evidence behind each date explicit, whereby a date confirmed by several independent contemporary listings is no longer recorded in the same form as an estimate, or in the same form as a date transmitted from another collection and never subsequently validated.

A single case demonstrates the method in operation. Six independent contemporary listings displace the recording's accepted date by almost seven years, and the day of the week cannot resolve the question, because both candidate dates fall on a Sunday and the program was broadcast on Sundays.

The paper also reports a single significant limitation. Within the sample analyzed, the number of listings available for a broadcast increases sharply with the year across the 1930s, a trend measured as a correlation of 0.899 across fourteen records. The evidence is not uniformly distributed across the period, and any dating framework must indicate the variation in evidence rather than obscure the variation behind a uniform claim of fact.
**Keywords:** old-time radio, discography, broadcast dating, newspaper radio logs, provenance, audio archives, metadata

sec.title: 1. The problem: a body of evidence that lost its dates
1. The problem: a body of evidence whose dates are lost
sec.p: Old American radio survives mainly because collectors saved old American radio. People recorded the programs on transcription discs and later on tape. People copied the copies. People traded the copies, and in time made the copies into computer files. The trading went on for about seventy years. Across seventy years, no library and no archive set a rule for the information that traveled with each recording. The result is a large body of valuable history with almost no reliable record keeping.

The clearest failure is the date. A recording without a date is much weaker as evidence. A reader cannot place an undated recording against the news of the week. A reader cannot connect an undated recording to an advertiser's campaign. A reader cannot say where an undated recording falls inside a program's run. A reader cannot use an undated recording to show what a network really broadcast on a given night. Radio was live and scheduled, and then radio was gone. So the date is not a detail among many. The date is what turns a sound file into a historical document.
Dates disappear in several different ways. Separating the ways helps, because each way needs a different answer.

**File names break down.** In trading networks, the file name carries the information. People write the file name again at every transfer to fit a new collector's system. Computers cut long file names short. Some letters are not legal on some computers, so people remove the letters. Computer programs for cataloging change other letters. A date written as `xx-xx-xx` may survive a single copy. A date written as `xx-xx-xx` does not survive three copies.

**Wrong dates are passed along.** When a date is present, the date is often passed along rather than proved. A collector chooses a date that looks reasonable. Every later collector copies the chosen date forward. Over time the chosen date starts to look official, only because so many collectors repeat the chosen date. Nothing in a trading network ever removes a wrong date.

**Programs are dated, but recordings are not.** Many holdings carry only the years a program ran, such as 1952 to 1961. A run of years is a fact about the program. A run of years is not a fact about the recording.

**Chosen dates are stored as facts.** When a cataloger is not sure, the chosen date goes into the same field, in the same form, as a proved date. Nothing marks the difference between a chosen date and a proved date. So the difference disappears at the first copy.

The paper treats the last failure as the main problem, because a careful method can repair the last failure. The Association for Recorded Sound Collections states the principle clearly in *Guidelines for Discographies*: "estimates are preferable to omitting the information. Discographers should explain the rationale behind estimates, and clearly distinguish them from 'solid' data."1 The rule is not that every date must be sure. The rule is that a reader must be able to see which dates are sure, and why.

American radio survives principally because private collectors retained the recordings. The programs were recorded on transcription discs and subsequently on tape, the copies were themselves copied, the copies were traded, and the traded copies were eventually converted into digital files. The sequence of copying and trading continued for approximately seventy years, and throughout seven decades no library or archive imposed a uniform convention on the documentation accompanying each recording. The result is a large body of historically significant material carrying almost no reliable documentation.

The most significant failure is the loss of the date. An undated recording is significantly weaker as evidence, because an undated recording cannot be assessed against the news of a particular week, linked to an advertiser's campaign, or located within the run of the program responsible for generating the recording. Nor can an undated recording demonstrate what a network in fact transmitted on a given evening. Radio was live and scheduled, and then radio was gone; the date is therefore not an attribute among many, but the attribute converting a sound file into a historical document.
Dates are lost through several distinct mechanisms, and separating the mechanisms is useful, because each mechanism requires a different response.

**File names break down.** Within trading networks the file name carries the documentation. Participants revise the name at each transfer to conform to local convention, operating systems reduce names exceeding a length limit, and characters illegal on a given platform are removed by the person transferring the file. Cataloging software alters the remaining characters. A date written as `xx-xx-xx` may survive a single transfer; a date written as `xx-xx-xx` does not survive three.

**Erroneous dates are transmitted forward.** Where a date is present the date has more often been transmitted than validated. A collector assigns a plausible date, and every subsequent recipient of the file copies the assigned date forward. The assigned date acquires an appearance of authority in direct proportion to the number of repetitions, and no mechanism within a trading network ever eliminates an erroneous date.

**Programs are dated; recordings are not.** Many holdings record only the years across which the program ran, for example 1952 to 1961. A range of years is a fact about the program, and a range of years is not a fact about the recording.

**Estimates are stored as facts.** When a cataloger estimates a date, the estimate is written into the same field, in the same format, as a validated date. Nothing marks the difference, and the difference is therefore lost at the first transfer.

The present paper treats the storage of estimates as facts as the principal problem, because a careful method can correct the storage of estimates as facts. The Association for Recorded Sound Collections states the principle explicitly in the association's *Guidelines for Discographies*: "estimates are preferable to omitting the information. Discographers should explain the rationale behind estimates, and clearly distinguish them from 'solid' data."1 The requirement is not conclusiveness in every date; the requirement is the reader's capacity to identify which dates are secure, and on what grounds.

sec.title: 1.1 What the existing guide books do, and what the guide books cannot do
1.1 What the existing reference works do, and what the reference works cannot do
sec.p: The field already has good guide books. John Dunning's *On the Air: The Encyclopedia of Old-Time Radio* describes about 1,500 programs. *On the Air* gives broadcast histories, times, networks, advertisers, and main workers.2 The *Handbook of Old-Time Radio*, by Jon Swartz and Robert Reinehr, serves collectors in a similar way.3 Together *On the Air* and the *Handbook of Old-Time Radio* establish the record at the level of the *program*, and establish the record well. The method described here depends on the work in both guide books. Step 2 of the procedure in section 4 uses a guide book to learn a program's usual day and hour.

But the guide books do not date a single surviving recording, and the guide books never set out to do so. The subject of the guide books is the program and the program's run. The problem here is the single item — a sound file, in trading now, whose place inside a program's run is not known. A guide book can tell a cataloger that *Greatest Story Ever Told* was a Sunday program, and that *Greatest Story Ever Told* ran in 1948 and also in 1955. A guide book cannot say which Sunday produced the recording a cataloger holds. In the case studied in section 5.4, the program-level record fits the correct date and the wrong date equally well.

So the hole is built into the problem. The hole is not a failure of the guide books. To date a single item, a cataloger needs evidence about the single item. For the old-time radio period, the only published record that works item by item, day by day, is the newspaper radio log. The paper argues that the newspaper radio log should be treated as the primary source for dating old radio recordings. The paper also argues that each record should show which listings a cataloger read, and what the listings proved.

The field already possesses authoritative reference works. John Dunning's *On the Air: The Encyclopedia of Old-Time Radio* documents approximately 1,500 programs, together with the broadcast histories, the scheduled times, the networks, the sponsors, and the principal contributors of the 1,500 programs.2 The *Handbook of Old-Time Radio*, by Jon Swartz and Robert Reinehr, serves the collecting community in a comparable capacity.3 Dunning and Swartz and Reinehr together establish the record at the level of the *program*, and Dunning and Swartz and Reinehr establish the record authoritatively. The method specified here depends on the work of Dunning and of Swartz and Reinehr: step 2 of the procedure in section 4 consults precisely the encyclopedic category of source in order to obtain a program's scheduled day and hour.

Dunning and Swartz and Reinehr do not, however, date an individual surviving recording, and the reference works were never designed to do so. The subject of Dunning and of Swartz and Reinehr is the program and the program's run, whereas the problem addressed here is the individual item — a single sound file, currently in distribution, whose position within the program's run is unknown. A reference work can indicate to a cataloger the status of *Greatest Story Ever Told* as a Sunday program broadcast in 1948 and again in 1955, but a reference work cannot specify which Sunday generated the recording in hand. In the case analyzed in section 5.4, the program-level record is equally consistent with the correct date and with the erroneous date.

The limitation of the reference works is therefore structural, and the limitation does not constitute a failure of the existing literature. Dating an individual item requires evidence about the individual item, and for the classic period of American radio the only published record operating at the level of the individual item, day by day, is the newspaper radio log. The present paper argues for treating the newspaper radio log as the primary source for dating undated recordings, and for making explicit in each record which listings were consulted and what the consulted listings establish.

sec.title: 2. The collection
2. The collection
sec.p: The Archive of American Radio is a public catalog of American broadcast recordings, and runs not for profit. In September 2026 The Archive of American Radio published 259,915 separate broadcast records across 6,114 programs.4 Every broadcast record has a fixed web address in the form `/series/{program}/episodes/{item}`. Where evidence has been found, a broadcast record also carries a formal citation, a set of newspaper listings, and a set of trade magazine listings.

The collection did not arrive all at once. The collection gathers material from the main old-time radio distribution channels, and so carries every dating problem described above, at full strength. Much of the cataloging work puts aside a date passed along and never tested with a date proved against published evidence from the time.
Two facts about the published catalog can be measured directly. Both facts matter for the method.

**For the classic period, the evidence is nearly complete.** The Archive of American Radio holds sixty records, chosen at random, whose item name carries a date between 1930 and 1959. Fifty-nine of the sixty records — 98 percent — carry at least one newspaper page image or trade magazine page image.5 For the years when the American radio log was a daily feature, the evidence the method needs is almost always present.

**Old dates survive beside corrected dates.** Of the 259,915 records, 44,566 carry a date in the item name, in the form `YYYY-MM-DD`, passed along from the file name of a source collection. In a random sample of forty date-carrying records from the whole collection, two records — 5 percent — carry a name date that does not agree with the broadcast date the record states. Inside the 1930 to 1959 window, a single record in sixty did not agree.6 Both samples are small, and both numbers should be read only as a rough size. Together the two samples suggest that one to two thousand records still carry an old date in the item name after the catalog has corrected the date. Section 5.4 examines a record in the same state.

**More than a quarter of the collection has no date at all.** In a random sample of 150 records from the whole catalog, 108 records — 72 percent — carry a broadcast date. Forty-two records — 28 percent — carry no date.7 Across 259,915 records, forty-two in 150 points to about seventy-two thousand items held with no date.

The link between dating and evidence in the same sample is the more useful result. Of the 108 records with dates, 101 records — 93.5 percent — carry at least one page image. Of the forty-two records without dates, **two** carry a page image. So records without dates are not, as a rule, records where a cataloger looked for evidence and failed. Records without dates are records where no cataloger has looked yet. In The Archive of American Radio, dating a record and gathering evidence for the record are nearly the same job. The forty records in the sample with no date and no evidence stand for work still to be done, and not for a limit on what the method can reach.

The Archive of American Radio is a public, not-for-profit catalog of American broadcast recordings. In September 2026 The Archive of American Radio published 259,915 discrete broadcast records distributed across 6,114 programs.4 Every broadcast record occupies a persistent address of the form `/series/{program}/episodes/{item}`, and, where the evidence permits, each record also carries a formatted citation, a set of newspaper listings, and a set of trade press listings.

The collection was not assembled at a single time. The Archive of American Radio aggregates material from the principal old-time radio distribution channels, and The Archive of American Radio consequently exhibits every dating failure specified above, at full strength. A significant proportion of the cataloging effort consists of replacing a transmitted, unvalidated date with a date established against contemporary published evidence.
Two properties of the published catalog can be measured directly, and both are significant for the method.

**For the classic period the available evidence is nearly complete.** The archive holds sixty records, selected at random, whose item name carries a date between 1930 and 1959. Fifty-nine of the sixty records — 98 percent — carry at least one newspaper or trade press page image.5 For the years in which the American newspaper radio log was a daily feature, the evidence the method requires is almost invariably available.

**Earlier dates persist alongside corrected dates.** Of the 259,915 records, 44,566 carry a date in the item name, in the form `YYYY-MM-DD`, transmitted from the file name of a source collection. In a random sample of forty date-carrying names taken from the whole collection, two — 5 percent — carry a name date inconsistent with the broadcast date the record itself specifies. Within the 1930 to 1959 interval, one record in sixty was inconsistent.6 Both samples are small, and the proportions should be read only as approximate. Taken together the two samples indicate a residue of one to two thousand records still carrying an earlier date in the name after the catalog has corrected the broadcast date, and section 5.4 analyzes a single inconsistent record in detail.

**More than a quarter of the collection is undated.** In a random sample of 150 records taken from the whole catalog, 108 — 72 percent — carry a broadcast date, and forty-two — 28 percent — carry none.7 Across 259,915 records, a 28 percent proportion indicates approximately seventy-two thousand items held without a date.

The correspondence between dating and evidence within the sample of 150 records is the more useful result. Of the 108 dated records, 101 — 93.5 percent — carry at least one page image, whereas of the 42 undated records, **two** carry a page image. Undated records are not, as a category, records in which evidence was sought and not found; undated records are records no cataloger has yet examined. In The Archive of American Radio, dating a record and assembling the record's evidence constitute very nearly the same operation. The forty records in the sample carrying neither a date nor any evidence therefore represent work still to be undertaken, and not a limit on the reach of the method.

sec.title: 2.1 The same broadcast, held more than once
2.1 The same broadcast, held more than once
sec.p: The published catalog shows a connected problem. The Archive of American Radio holds three separate records for Winston Churchill's speech on Anglo-American unity, given at Harvard on 6 September 1943. Two records carry the date Monday, 6 September 1943, and six page images each. The third record carries no date and no evidence at all.8

Three records for a single broadcast is normal for a collection built from trading. The same broadcast arrives by several routes, and each copy carries a different amount of information. Removing the extra copies is itself a dating problem. The record without a date is a weak record whose answer The Archive of American Radio already holds, completely proved, in two records cataloged separately. Sorting out a group of copies is among the most useful work a cataloger can do, because the evidence has already been found.

The published catalog exhibits an analogous problem. The archive holds three discrete records for Winston Churchill's speech on Anglo-American unity, delivered at Harvard on 6 September 1943. Two of the three records carry the date Monday, 6 September 1943, together with six page images each, whereas the third record carries neither a date nor any supporting evidence.8

Duplication of a single broadcast is normal in a collection aggregated from trading networks. The same broadcast arrives by several routes, and each copy carries a different volume of supporting documentation, so resolving the copies against each other is itself a dating problem. The undated Churchill record is an impoverished record whose answer The Archive of American Radio already holds, fully validated, in the two Churchill records cataloged separately. Resolving a duplicated group of records is among the most productive tasks available to a cataloger, precisely because the underlying evidence has already been obtained.

sec.title: 3. Kinds of evidence
3. Kinds of evidence
sec.p: Three kinds of evidence can fix the date of a surviving broadcast recording. The three kinds are not the same in how often each exists, in how exact each is, and in the kind of mistake each invites. A method that treats the three kinds as equal will produce wrong answers that look sure.

Three categories of evidence are capable of establishing the date of a surviving broadcast recording. The three categories differ in frequency of survival, in precision, and in the characteristic error each category invites. A method treating the three categories as equivalent will generate erroneous conclusions carrying an appearance of certainty.

sec.title: 3.1 Newspaper radio logs
3.1 Newspaper radio logs
sec.p: The newspaper radio log is the main kind. From the early 1930s, large American daily newspapers printed a day-by-day radio schedule, called the radio log. The radio log listed the station, the time, and the program name for the coming day. Radio logs are the closest thing the period produced to a complete published record of what went on the air.

Four newspapers carry the method: the *New York Times*, the *Washington Post*, the *Chicago Daily Tribune*, and the *Los Angeles Times*. The value of the four newspapers comes less from any single newspaper than from the fact that the four newspapers are separate. Each newspaper built a radio log from information supplied separately by networks and stations, for a different city and a different time zone. A program name and hour printed in all four newspapers is confirmed in a way a single listing can never be.

Radio logs have three weaknesses, and each weakness must be answered openly. First, a radio log records the *schedule* — what a network meant to broadcast — and not the *broadcast*. When a news bulletin went out instead, the radio log and the broadcast no longer agree. Second, the radio log went to the printer before the broadcast day began, so the radio log shows an earlier deadline. Third, radio logs are printed in very small print in narrow newspaper columns. Computers read small print badly, so mistakes enter easily.

The newspaper radio log constitutes the primary category. From the early 1930s onward, the major American daily newspapers printed a day-by-day radio schedule, designated the radio log. The radio log specified the station, the hour, and the program name for the subsequent broadcast day. Newspaper radio logs approximate, more closely than any other published series, a complete contemporary record of American broadcast transmission.

Four newspapers sustain the method: the *New York Times*, the *Washington Post*, the *Chicago Daily Tribune*, and the *Los Angeles Times*. The value of the four newspapers derives less from the authority of any individual newspaper than from the mutual independence of the four newspapers. Each newspaper compiled a radio log from information supplied separately by networks and stations, for a distinct city within a distinct time zone. A program name and hour printed in all four newspapers is corroborated in a manner no individual listing can achieve.

Newspaper radio logs exhibit three weaknesses, and each weakness requires an explicit response. First, a radio log documents the *schedule* — the transmission a network intended — and not the *broadcast*. Where a news bulletin displaced the scheduled program, the radio log and the broadcast diverge. Second, the radio log went to press before the broadcast day commenced, so the radio log reflects an earlier deadline. Third, newspaper radio logs were printed in very small type within narrow columns. Automated text recognition performs poorly on small type, so transcription errors enter the evidence readily.

sec.title: 3.2 Trade magazines
3.2 Trade magazines
sec.p: *Broadcasting*, the industry weekly magazine, and magazines like *Broadcasting*, recorded changes to schedules, advertiser assignments, network line-ups, and special events. Trade magazines give a kind of detail the daily newspapers never tried to give. Trade coverage is weekly, not daily, and so covers fewer dates. But trade coverage is much richer in the detail that separates a broadcast from another broadcast inside a program's run. Trade coverage is the natural second source when a radio log proves a program aired, but not which episode aired.

*Broadcasting*, the weekly periodical of the American broadcasting industry, together with comparable weekly periodicals, documented schedule alterations, advertiser assignments, network line-ups, and special events. Trade periodicals supply a category of detail the daily newspapers never attempted to supply. Trade coverage appears weekly rather than daily, and trade coverage therefore addresses a smaller proportion of individual dates. Trade coverage is, however, substantially richer in precisely the detail distinguishing a single broadcast from an adjacent broadcast within a program's run. Trade coverage constitutes the natural secondary source wherever a newspaper radio log establishes the transmission of a program without establishing which episode was transmitted.

sec.title: 3.3 Evidence inside the recording
3.3 Evidence inside the recording
sec.p: A recording contains information that can be dated. A word about the news sets an earliest possible date. An advertiser's words, and the campaign named in the words, can be placed inside a season. The announcer's name, the network's wording, and the wording of station identification all changed over time, and every change can be dated. Sometimes a broadcast names a current event. A broadcast may give an election result, a war report, or the result of a game. Then the recording can often be placed to the exact day from what the recording says. No outside listing is needed.

Evidence inside a recording is the only kind that speaks to the *broadcast* rather than the schedule. So evidence inside a recording decides the question when a radio log and a recording do not agree. Evidence inside a recording is also the kind most easily mixed up by a later repeat, a later copy, or an Armed Forces Radio Service reissue of the same program.

A recording contains internal information capable of supporting a date. A reference to the news establishes an earliest possible date. An advertiser's copy, together with the campaign identified in the copy, can be located within a commercial season. The announcer's name, the network's formal wording, and the wording of station identification all altered over time, and every alteration is datable. A broadcast occasionally names a current event, reporting an election result, a war dispatch, or the outcome of a sporting contest. Where a current event is named, the recording can frequently be located to the exact day from the recording's own content, and no external listing is required.

Evidence internal to a recording is the only category speaking to the *broadcast* rather than to the schedule. Evidence internal to a recording therefore adjudicates the question wherever a newspaper radio log and a recording diverge. Evidence internal to a recording is also the category most readily confounded by a subsequent repeat, a subsequent copy, or an Armed Forces Radio Service reissue of the same program.

sec.title: 4. The method
4. The method
sec.p: The whole method is one sentence. Ignore the date on the file, work out roughly which week the recording is from, look that week up in the newspaper radio listings, and count how many of the four newspapers list it. The count is how sure you get to be.
The rest of this section is why each step is there.

**Ignore the date on the file.** The date on a file name was put there by someone you cannot ask. Start from that date and the work quietly changes shape: instead of asking what night the show went out, you start looking for a reason to keep the date you were handed. And you will find one, because a plausible date usually has a plausible story around it. So write the date down, mark where it came from, and set it aside. Do not use it again until the end.

**Work out roughly when the recording was made.** Listen to it. A war report, an election result, a sports score, a joke about the news — any of these can fix the week. The advertising helps too, because campaigns ran in seasons. So does the announcer, and so does the wording of the station identification, which changed over the years. None of this gives a day. It gives a window, and a window is enough to go looking.

**Look that week up in the newspaper radio listings.** Every big American daily printed the next day's radio schedule: station, time, show. Four papers matter here — the *New York Times*, the *Washington Post*, the *Chicago Daily Tribune*, the *Los Angeles Times*. Read the listings for each candidate date, in each paper.
**Count the newspapers that list the show at the same hour.** The count is the answer, and it becomes the mark on the record:
sec.list: - **A** — two or more newspapers list the broadcast - **B** — one newspaper lists the broadcast - **C** — no newspaper lists the broadcast, but the recording and the show's known schedule point to the same date - **D** — an estimate, given as a range, with the reasoning written down - **E** — the date came with the file and nobody has checked it
sec.p: Counting works because the four papers are separate. Each built its listings in its own city, in its own time zone, from copy the networks sent to each paper on its own. Four papers agreeing is four people who never spoke to each other saying the same thing. That is why two is the line for Mark A.

**Mark E is the one that matters.** A catalog with no way to write down "nobody has checked this" will turn a stranger's guess into a fact, and will do it silently. Section 5.4 is exactly that: 13 February 1955 never had evidence behind it. It had repetition behind it.

Two things to watch. Two papers printing the same network schedule are one source, not two — the network wrote it once. And a recording that fits a listing may still be a later repeat, so check whether the advertising has been cut out, because that is what the Armed Forces Radio Service did when it reissued a show.

sec.title: 5.1 A broadcast with a great deal of evidence: 1 September 1939
5.1 A broadcast supported by abundant evidence: 1 September 1939
sec.p: The BBC announcer Alvar Lidell reported the German invasion of Poland. The Archive of American Radio holds the report as a recording of forty-five seconds.9 The catalog record for the Alvar Lidell report carries ten separate page images. The ten page images include radio logs from the *Chicago Daily Tribune*, the *New York Times*, and the *Los Angeles Times*. The ten page images also include two different listings from the *Washington Post*. All the listings are for Friday 1 September 1939. The same issue of *Broadcasting* completes the set.10

The Alvar Lidell date is a Mark A date by a wide margin. The Alvar Lidell record shows the best the method can do. A broadcast that mattered around the world, on a day that mattered around the world, is listed everywhere, and confirming the date is easy.

The BBC announcer Alvar Lidell reported the German invasion of Poland. The Archive of American Radio holds the Alvar Lidell report as a recording of forty-five seconds.9 The catalog record for the Alvar Lidell report carries ten separate page images. The ten page images comprise newspaper radio logs from the *Chicago Daily Tribune*, the *New York Times*, and the *Los Angeles Times*, together with two distinct listings from the *Washington Post*. Every listing is dated Friday, 1 September 1939. The corresponding issue of *Broadcasting* completes the set.10

The Alvar Lidell date constitutes a Mark A date by a wide margin. The Alvar Lidell record demonstrates the maximum the method is able to achieve. A broadcast of global significance, transmitted on a day of global significance, is listed universally, and confirmation of the date is correspondingly straightforward.

sec.title: 5.2 The same day, a different recording
5.2 The same day, a different recording
sec.p: The Archive of American Radio catalogs Ignacy Jan Paderewski's speech about the coming German invasion separately, on the same day. The Paderewski record rests on the same group of evidence: a *Chicago Daily Tribune* radio log for Friday 1 September 1939, and the same issue of *Broadcasting*.11 The Alvar Lidell record and the Paderewski record are useful together for what the two records show about method. A single group of listings for a single day can support several separate broadcast records. The single piece of evidence is the printed page, and not the recording.

The Archive of American Radio catalogs Ignacy Jan Paderewski's speech concerning the impending German invasion separately, on the identical day. The Paderewski record rests on the same aggregate of evidence: a *Chicago Daily Tribune* radio log for Friday, 1 September 1939, together with the corresponding issue of *Broadcasting*.11 The Alvar Lidell record and the Paderewski record are instructive in combination for what the two records demonstrate about method. A single aggregate of listings for a single day is capable of supporting several distinct broadcast records. The unit of evidence is the printed page, and not the recording.

sec.title: 5.3 A broadcast with little evidence: 1932
5.3 A broadcast supported by sparse evidence: 1932
sec.p: Now compare a recording from 1932. The record for Franz von Papen's speech as chancellor, on 13 August 1932, carries three page images. The three page images come from the *New York Times* and the *Washington Post* only.12 The *Chicago Daily Tribune* listing and the *Los Angeles Times* listing that support the 1939 records are missing. The von Papen date is supported, but the confirmation behind the von Papen date is much less. A system that reported the Alvar Lidell record and the von Papen record the same way would give a false picture of the von Papen record.

Consider, by contrast, a recording from 1932. The record for Franz von Papen's speech as chancellor, delivered on 13 August 1932, carries three page images, and the three page images derive from the *New York Times* and the *Washington Post* alone.12 The *Chicago Daily Tribune* listing and the *Los Angeles Times* listing supporting the 1939 records are absent. The von Papen date is supported, but the corroboration behind the von Papen date is substantially weaker. A framework reporting the Alvar Lidell record and the von Papen record in an identical form would misrepresent the von Papen record.

sec.title: 5.4 A case that corrects a passed-along date by seven years
5.4 A case correcting a transmitted date by seven years
sec.p: The value of the method lies in correction, and not in repetition. A clear case is the *Greatest Story Ever Told* episode "They Did Not Receive Him."

The recording is traded under a file name holding the date 13 February 1955. The 1955 date also survives in the item name inside The Archive of American Radio, passed along from the source collection. But the catalog record gives the broadcast date as **Sunday, 29 February 1948** — an error of almost seven years in the traded date.13

Six separate listings from the time support the 1948 date. The six listings are radio logs in the *New York Times*, the *Washington Post*, the *Los Angeles Times*, and the *Chicago Daily Tribune*. A separate "Radio Highlights" item in the *Chicago Daily Tribune* is the fifth listing. The matching issue of *Broadcasting* is the sixth listing. All six listings are for Sunday, 29 February 1948.14 The date for "They Did Not Receive Him" is a Mark A date.
Two features make the *Greatest Story Ever Told* case worth studying.

First, **the day of the week cannot settle the case.** *Greatest Story Ever Told* was a Sunday program, and both possible dates fall on a Sunday. Both 13 February 1955 and 29 February 1948 were Sundays. A method resting on a program's known weekday would have accepted the passed-along date without trouble. Only the six supporting listings tell the two possible dates from each other. The *Greatest Story Ever Told* case is the argument for requiring published evidence instead of reasoning from a schedule.

Second, **the correct date is a leap day.** 29 February 1948 exists only because 1948 was a leap year. Leap days are a known source of passed-along mistakes. A cataloger putting a date back together from a damaged or partial file name will usually change a strange-looking 02-29 into a date that looks usual. The error in the *Greatest Story Ever Told* record runs in exactly the direction a leap day predicts.

The citation inside The Archive of American Radio already points to a web address without the wrong date. So the corrected date is what the catalog states and cites. The 1955 text survives only in the item name — an example of the file name problem described in section 1, now repeated inside a catalog that has otherwise corrected the date.
The value of the method resides in correction, and not in the confirmation of an already accepted answer. A clear instance is the *Greatest Story Ever Told* episode "They Did Not Receive Him."

The recording circulates under a file name carrying the date 13 February 1955. The 1955 date also survives in the item name within The Archive of American Radio, transmitted from the source collection. The catalog record, however, specifies the broadcast date as **Sunday, 29 February 1948** — an error of almost seven years in the traded date.13

Six independent contemporary listings support the 1948 date. The six listings comprise newspaper radio logs in the *New York Times*, the *Washington Post*, the *Los Angeles Times*, and the *Chicago Daily Tribune*. A separate "Radio Highlights" item in the *Chicago Daily Tribune* constitutes the fifth listing, and the corresponding issue of *Broadcasting* constitutes the sixth listing. All six listings are dated Sunday, 29 February 1948.14 The date for the episode is therefore a Mark A date.
Two features render the *Greatest Story Ever Told* case worth extended analysis.

First, **the day of the week cannot resolve the case.** *Greatest Story Ever Told* was a Sunday program, and both candidate dates fall on a Sunday. 13 February 1955 and 29 February 1948 were both Sundays. A method resting on a program's established weekday would have accepted the transmitted date without difficulty. Only the six supporting listings discriminate between the two candidate dates. The *Greatest Story Ever Told* case therefore constitutes the argument for requiring published evidence in place of inference from a schedule.

Second, **the correct date is a leap day.** 29 February 1948 exists only because 1948 was a leap year. Leap days are an established source of transmitted error. A cataloger reconstructing a date from a damaged or partial file name will ordinarily convert an anomalous 02-29 into a date of conventional appearance. The error within the *Greatest Story Ever Told* record runs in exactly the direction a leap day predicts.

The citation within The Archive of American Radio already resolves to an address free of the erroneous date, so the corrected date is the date the catalog states and cites. The 1955 text survives only within the item name — an instance of the file name problem specified in section 1, now reproduced inside a catalog having otherwise corrected the broadcast date.

sec.title: 6. The evidence is not equally thick across the period
6. Evidence density across the period
sec.p: The three examples above suggest a shape, and the shape can be measured. The Archive of American Radio holds fourteen cataloged broadcasts from a single news program, covering 1932 to 1939. Across the fourteen broadcasts, the number of separate page images attached to a record rises strongly with the year of the broadcast. The correlation is 0.899 across fourteen records.15 The mean number of page images by year:

Two reasons are possible, and the measurements cannot separate the two reasons. The first reason is that newspaper radio logs really did grow across the 1930s, as radio became a mass medium and the radio log grew from a new thing into a fixed daily feature. The second reason is that collecting of newspaper images by The Archive of American Radio is simply more complete for the later 1930s. Under the second reason, the shape describes the archive and not the period.

The difference between the two reasons matters for how the marks should be read. Under the first reason, a Mark B date from 1932 is as strong as the evidence of 1932 permits. Under the second reason, a Mark B date from 1932 is only a record The Archive of American Radio has not finished working on. Telling the two reasons apart would require a newspaper index independent of the archive's own holdings. No one has read an independent index.

The finding is limited in another way as well. The finding rests on fourteen records, all from a single program of international news. International news is exactly the kind of program most likely to appear in every city's radio log. A general statement about the whole collection would need a sample spread across program kinds and networks.

The finding is limited in a further respect. The finding rests on fourteen records, all drawn from a single program of international news, and international news is precisely the category of program most likely to appear in every city's radio log. sec.title: 7. Limits
7. Limits
sec.p: **A schedule is not a broadcast.** Every date the method takes from a newspaper proves what was scheduled. Programs were pulled, above all during news events, and news events are exactly when the collection is richest and the reasoning weakest.

**Repeats and reissues.** A recording that agrees with a listing may be an Armed Forces Radio Service reissue, a regional repeat, or a later copy of the same program. Only evidence inside the recording can tell a reissue from a first broadcast, and evidence inside the recording is not always present.
**Computer reading errors.** Radio logs are printed in dense, small print. Computers read small print badly. A mistake in the evidence passes into the catalog with no sign.

**Small samples.** The finding in section 6 rests on fourteen records from a single program. The collection-wide numbers in section 2 come from the published catalog, and completing the numbers needs the cataloging history held by The Archive of American Radio.

**Copying the evidence.** For the old-time radio period, the newspaper pages that provide the evidence are still under copyright. The paper cites listings by newspaper, date, and kind of listing. The paper does not copy the newspaper pages.16

**A schedule is not a broadcast.** Every date the method derives from a newspaper establishes the scheduled transmission. Programs were displaced, above all during news events, and news events are precisely the occasions on which the collection is richest and the inference weakest.

**Repeats and reissues.** A recording consistent with a listing may constitute an Armed Forces Radio Service reissue, a regional repeat, or a subsequent copy of the same program. Only evidence internal to the recording is capable of distinguishing a reissue from an original transmission, and evidence internal to the recording is not invariably present.

**Automated transcription errors.** Newspaper radio logs were printed in dense, small type, and automated text recognition performs poorly on dense, small type. An error within the evidence passes into the catalog without any indication.

**Small samples.** The finding in section 6 rests on fourteen records drawn from a single program. The collection-wide proportions in section 2 derive from the published catalog, and completing the proportions requires the cataloging history held internally by The Archive of American Radio.

**Reproduction of the evidence.** For the classic period of American radio, the newspaper pages supplying the evidence remain under copyright. The present paper cites listings by newspaper, date, and category of listing, and the present paper does not reproduce the newspaper pages.16

sec.title: 8. Publishing the reasoning, not only the answer
8. Publishing the reasoning, not only the answer
sec.p: A mark for the strength of evidence solves nothing while the mark lives only in a cataloger's private notes. The failure described in section 1 is exactly that careful decisions flatten into bare claims as recordings pass from collector to collector. For a mark to survive the trading networks that will pass old radio recordings on, the mark must be published with the record and attached to the record firmly.
Three rules follow. The Archive of American Radio follows all three rules.

**The citation belongs to the record, and not to a report.** Each broadcast record carries a formatted citation and a list of supporting listings beside the date, at the same web address. A reader who reaches a broadcast record reaches the evidence for the record. Publishing the citation beside the date is what makes the undated copy in section 2.1 easy to see. Two records state a date with six listings each. A third record states nothing. Any reader can see the difference.

**The item name must not carry a competing claim.** Section 5.4 is a warning. The catalog holds the corrected date, cites six listings for the corrected date, and points the citation at a web address without the wrong date. Yet the item name still reads `1955-02-13`, and the item name is what another computer reading web addresses will collect. An item name containing a date makes a claim, whether or not a cataloger meant a claim. The estimate in section 2 suggests one to two thousand records are in the same state. Dates belong in fields, and not in names.

**Missing information must be recordable.** Twenty-eight percent of the collection has no date, and the catalog says so rather than supplying a likely year. Saying so is the same rule the Association for Recorded Sound Collections asks of discographers in the passage quoted in section 1. For a date with no support, the other choice is not an empty space to fill in. The other choice is a clear statement that the question is still open. Mark E holds the statement. The number of two in forty-two — records without dates almost never carrying page images — is what makes Mark E useful, because the number identifies undated records as work waiting to be done.

A mark for the strength of evidence resolves nothing while the mark resides only in a cataloger's private notes. The failure specified in section 1 is precisely the flattening of careful decisions into bare assertions as recordings pass from collector to collector. For a mark to survive the trading networks destined to carry American radio recordings forward, the mark must be published alongside the record and attached to the record durably.
Three requirements follow, and The Archive of American Radio implements all three requirements.

**The citation belongs to the record, and not to a report.** Each broadcast record carries a formatted citation and a list of supporting listings beside the date, at the identical web address. A reader reaching a broadcast record reaches the evidence for the broadcast record. Publishing the citation beside the date is the mechanism rendering the undated copy in section 2.1 immediately visible. Two records state a date supported by six page images each, whereas a third record states nothing, and any reader is able to perceive the difference.

**The item name must not carry a competing claim.** Section 5.4 constitutes a warning. The catalog holds the corrected date, cites six listings for the corrected date, and directs the citation at an address free of the erroneous date. The item name nevertheless still reads `1955-02-13`, and the item name is the text an automated agent reading web addresses will aggregate. An item name containing a date advances a claim, irrespective of the cataloger's intention. The estimate in section 2 indicates a residue of one to two thousand records in an identical state. Dates belong in fields, and not in names.

**Absent information must be recordable.** Twenty-eight percent of the collection carries no date, and the catalog states the absence rather than supplying a plausible year. The explicit statement of absence is the requirement the Association for Recorded Sound Collections imposes on discographers in the passage quoted in section 1. For a date lacking support, the alternative is not an empty space awaiting completion. The alternative is an explicit statement that the question remains open, and Mark E carries the statement. The proportion of two in forty-two — undated records almost never carrying page images — is the measurement rendering Mark E useful, because the proportion identifies undated records as work awaiting completion.

sec.title: 9. Conclusion
9. Conclusion
sec.p: The dating problem in old-time radio is not mainly a problem of missing evidence. The evidence largely exists. The evidence sits in the radio logs of four large daily newspapers and in the trade press, and most of the evidence is now on computers. The problem is that the information kept with old radio recordings has no way to show the difference between a date proved against published evidence and a date passed along without evidence. So a proved date and a passed along date can no longer be told from each other.

The answer offered here is simple. Attach a mark for the strength of evidence to every date. Keep a visible category for dates passed along and never tested. Cite the exact published listing behind every confirmed date. Applied across 259,915 records, the marking system turns a trading collection into a collection scholars can cite.

The dating problem in American radio is not principally a problem of absent evidence, because the evidence largely survives. The evidence resides in the newspaper radio logs of four major daily newspapers and in the trade press, and the greater proportion of the evidence is now available in digital form. The problem is that the documentation accompanying American radio recordings possesses no mechanism for expressing the difference between a date validated against contemporary published evidence and a date transmitted without evidence. A validated date and a transmitted date are consequently no longer distinguishable from each other.

The remedy proposed here is straightforward. Attach a mark for the strength of evidence to every date. Maintain a visible category for dates transmitted and never validated. Cite the exact published listing behind every confirmed date. Applied across 259,915 records, the marking framework converts a trading collection into a collection scholars are able to cite.

sec.title: Sources for the discography
Sources for the discography
sec.p: This section states the sources the method rests on, what each one covers, and where the coverage fails, so that a reader can follow the same steps described in section 4.

**Newspaper radio logs.** Four large daily newspapers carry this method: the *New York Times* (New York), the *Washington Post* (Washington), the *Chicago Daily Tribune* (Chicago), and the *Los Angeles Times* (Los Angeles). Each built its log from information supplied for its own city and time zone. That is why agreement between them counts as confirmation rather than repetition. Where a newspaper printed both, two kinds of listing are counted separately: the daily *radio log*, which is a complete schedule, and *radio highlights*, which is a selected column written by an editor. The *Chicago Daily Tribune* record for 29 February 1948, discussed in section 5.4, provides one of each, and they count as two listings because they were produced separately.

Coverage is not even. Within the archive's holdings, the number of listings available for a broadcast rises across the 1930s, from an average of 3.0 in 1932 to 7.8 in 1939 in the sample studied (section 6). For the years 1930 to 1959, 98 percent of the cataloged broadcasts sampled carry at least one page image. Across the whole collection the figure is 68.7 percent. Almost all of that difference comes from records with no date, of which only two in forty-two carry any page image at all.

**Where the newspaper images came from.** The catalog presents each newspaper listing as a page image, labeled with the newspaper, the city, the date, and the kind of listing. It does not record where the scan came from. The published version of this paper should name that source. It should say whether each run was read in a library newspaper database, on microfilm, or in a scan collection made by someone else. It should also say what is known about how complete that source is. Where the source is a private collection rather than a library, the paper should say so plainly. It should give what is known about the collection's history and about any rights it claims. A reader cannot follow steps whose starting point is unnamed, and recording it is the single most useful addition this apparatus still needs.

**Trade magazines.** *Broadcasting*, the industry weekly, is read through WorldRadioHistory, which the catalog names and cites as the source of the scan. Trade coverage is weekly rather than daily. It is used for schedule changes, advertiser assignments, network line-ups, and special events — that is, for separating one broadcast from another inside a run when the daily logs give only a program name. In the sample studied, *Broadcasting* appears for the better documented broadcasts and is missing for the thinner ones. It adds to the daily logs. It does not replace them.

**Evidence inside the recordings.** The recordings are the archive's own holdings. Each has a permanent web address in the form `/series/{program}/episodes/{item}`, and each carries a formal citation. Where this paper cites evidence inside a recording, it means sound that can be heard in the archive's copy.

**Where coverage fails.** Three failures are known, and any reader following this work should expect them. Radio logs record the schedule and not the broadcast, so a replaced program breaks the match — and that happens most often during news events, which is when this collection is richest. Logs went to press before the broadcast day began. And they are printed in dense, small type that computers read badly, so mistakes in the evidence pass silently into the catalog. Adding more newspapers does not fix any of these, because all four newspapers share them.

The present section specifies the sources the method depends upon, the coverage each source provides, and the points at which the coverage fails, so a reader is able to replicate the sequence of steps described in section 4.

**Newspaper radio logs.** Four major daily newspapers sustain the method: the *New York Times* (New York), the *Washington Post* (Washington), the *Chicago Daily Tribune* (Chicago), and the *Los Angeles Times* (Los Angeles). Each newspaper compiled a radio log from information supplied for the newspaper's own city and time zone. The independence of compilation is the reason agreement among the four newspapers constitutes corroboration rather than repetition. Where a newspaper printed both, two categories of listing are counted separately: the daily *radio log*, a complete schedule, and *radio highlights*, a selected column composed by an editor. The *Chicago Daily Tribune* record for 29 February 1948, analyzed in section 5.4, supplies a single instance of each category, and the two items count as two listings because the two items were produced independently.

Coverage is not uniform. Within the archive's holdings, the number of listings available for a broadcast increases across the 1930s, from a mean of 3.0 in 1932 to a mean of 7.8 in 1939 within the sample analyzed in section 6. For the years 1930 to 1959, 98 percent of the cataloged broadcasts sampled carry at least one page image, whereas across the whole collection the corresponding proportion is 68.7 percent. Almost the entire difference derives from records carrying no date, of which only two in forty-two carry any page image at all.

**The provenance of the newspaper images.** The catalog presents each newspaper listing as a page image, labeled with the newspaper, the city, the date, and the category of listing, and the catalog does not record the provenance of the scan. The published version of the present paper should name the provenance explicitly. The published version should specify whether each run was consulted in a library newspaper database, on microfilm, or within a scan collection assembled by a third party, and the published version should specify what is established about the completeness of the source. Where the source constitutes a private collection rather than a library, the paper should state the fact plainly, together with what is established about the collection's history and about any rights the collection asserts. A reader cannot replicate a sequence of steps whose starting point is unnamed, and recording the provenance is the single most useful addition the apparatus still requires.

**Trade magazines.** *Broadcasting*, the weekly periodical of the industry, is consulted through WorldRadioHistory, which the catalog names and cites as the source of the scan. Trade coverage is weekly rather than daily. Trade coverage supports schedule alterations, advertiser assignments, network line-ups, and special events — the category of detail distinguishing a single broadcast from an adjacent broadcast within a run wherever the daily newspaper radio logs supply only a program name. Within the sample analyzed, *Broadcasting* appears for the better documented broadcasts and is absent for the sparsely documented broadcasts. Trade coverage supplements the daily newspaper radio logs, and trade coverage does not replace the daily newspaper radio logs.

**Evidence inside the recordings.** The recordings constitute the archive's own holdings. Each recording occupies a persistent address of the form `/series/{program}/episodes/{item}`, and each recording carries a formal citation. Where the present paper cites evidence internal to a recording, the citation refers to sound audible within the archive's copy.

**Where coverage fails.** Three failures are established, and any reader replicating the present work should anticipate all three failures. Newspaper radio logs document the schedule rather than the broadcast, so a displaced program breaks the correspondence, and displacement occurs most frequently during news events, precisely when the collection is richest. Newspaper radio logs went to press before the broadcast day commenced. And newspaper radio logs were printed in dense, small type, which automated text recognition reads badly, so errors within the evidence pass silently into the catalog. Adding further newspapers corrects none of the three failures, because all four newspapers share all three failures.
